item.title: Wrist & Hand — Traction / Translatoric Glide
clinicalUse: Use when assessment identifies a relevant impairment in Wrist & Hand and the parent technique fits the patient's presentation.
Primary treatment target: wrist/hand range, grip, dexterity and task-related pain.
Retain the technique only if it produces a meaningful within-session improvement.
patientPosition: Sitting with forearm and hand supported on the table.
Keep fingers relaxed unless active movement is part of the technique.
therapistPosition: Sit or stand beside the hand so small contacts can be controlled precisely.
stabilization: Stabilize the forearm or adjacent carpal/metacarpal segment.
contact: Use small, broad contacts over the intended joint/tendon/muscle and avoid compressing superficial nerves or inflamed structures.
Stabilize one bone and contact the adjacent segment close to the joint line.
Use the treatment plane appropriate to the joint rather than pulling from a distant lever.
forceDirection: Traction is applied perpendicular to the treatment plane; glide is applied parallel to it.
Grade I reduces compression, Grade II takes up slack and Grade III provides a sustained stretch when appropriate.
dosage: Use brief sustained trials, often 10–30 seconds repeated 3–5 times, adjusted to irritability and response.
steps: 1. Record the exact comparable sign for Wrist & Hand: wrist/hand range, grip, dexterity and task-related pain.
2. Screen regional red flags, contraindications and technique-specific precautions before touching the patient.
3. Position and stabilize the patient so the target is comfortable and the manual input can be localized.
4. Apply a low-force trial using the parent technique principles and the region-specific contact described above.
5. Monitor pain quality, symptom distribution, guarding and patient confidence throughout.
6. Re-test the original comparable sign immediately after the trial.
7. Keep the technique only when the response is useful, then transfer the gain into active movement, loading or self-management.
mistakes: Applying the technique because it is familiar rather than because the examination supports it.
Using more force when the response is unclear or worsening.
Failing to re-test the exact movement or function that justified the treatment.
safety: Respect fracture, acute ligament injury, inflammatory flare, nerve compression and postoperative precautions.
Stop or modify if symptoms peripheralize, neurological status worsens, the response is disproportionate or the patient asks to stop.
item.visualCue: Wrist & Hand assessment → correct regional setup → Traction / Translatoric Glide → immediate comparable-sign re-test.

subTechniques.name: Radiocarpal Traction — Kaltenborn
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Reduce compression and prepare the wrist for translatoric glides.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Sitting with forearm supported and wrist just off the table.
subTechniques.contact: Stabilize distal radius/ulna and grasp the proximal carpal row/hand close to the joint.
subTechniques.direction: Apply sustained distraction perpendicular to the radiocarpal treatment plane.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: Traction should occur at the joint, not by pulling the fingers.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Avoid acute fracture or carpal instability.

subTechniques.name: Radiocarpal Dorsal / Volar Translatoric Glide
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Improve flexion or extension using a sustained translatoric glide.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Forearm supported with the wrist relaxed.
subTechniques.contact: Stabilize radius/ulna and contact the proximal carpal row.
subTechniques.direction: Use dorsal glide for flexion restriction or volar glide for extension restriction, then verify with re-test.
subTechniques.reassess: Wrist flexion/extension and the patient's task.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: Biomechanical direction is a starting hypothesis—the patient's response confirms whether the glide is worth keeping.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Respect ligament injury and postoperative precautions.
